debrief.goal: Replace the recurrent and convolutional layers of sequence-to-sequence models with attention alone, so training can run in parallel across positions and distant words are linked in a constant number of steps, while beating earlier translation quality at lower training cost.
debrief.approach: An encoder and a decoder, each a stack of 6 identical layers. Every layer has multi-head scaled dot-product attention and a position-wise feed-forward network, each wrapped in a residual connection plus layer normalization. The decoder adds attention over the encoder output and masks its self-attention so outputs depend only on earlier outputs. Sinusoidal positional encodings supply word order. Training uses Adam with a warmup-then-decay learning rate, residual dropout, and label smoothing.
debrief.use_yourself: Suggestions, not claims of the paper: scaled dot-product and multi-head attention as a reusable building block; the masking trick for any auto-regressive model; the warmup-then-inverse-square-root learning-rate schedule; label smoothing; checkpoint averaging; and the Table 1 style of comparing layers by cost, sequential steps, and path length.

quiz.answer: Recurrence (and convolution). Without them nothing carries word order, so the model needs positional encodings added to its inputs.
More work done in parallel. Recurrence forces O(n) sequential steps per layer; self-attention needs O(1). The paper does not claim fewer parameters or a new loss.
Yes. Transformer (big) scores 28.4 BLEU vs 26.36 for the best ensemble (ConvS2S), about 2 points higher. Even the base model (27.3) beats every listed ensemble.

(1) Encoder self-attention: queries, keys, values all from the previous encoder layer. (2) Decoder self-attention: all from the previous decoder layer, masked to earlier positions. (3) Encoder-decoder attention: queries from the previous decoder layer, keys and values from the encoder output.

The decoder generates outputs one at a time, so position i may only depend on outputs before i. Masking (scores set to −∞), together with shifting the output embeddings by one, enforces this. The encoder sees an input that is fully known, so it needs no mask.

It could not use word order, because nothing else in the model encodes position (Sec. 3.5). Example (illustration, not from the paper): 'the dog bit the man' vs 'the man bit the dog' contain the same tokens in a different order.
Variance is d_k = 64 (footnote 4). Dividing by √64 = 8 divides the variance by 64, bringing it back to 1. That is the 1/√d_k scaling.

Each head works in d_model/h = 64 dimensions, so 8 heads together cover 8 × 64 = 512, the same as one full-width head. The paper states the total cost is similar to single-head attention at full dimension.

Self-attention: n²·d = 2,500 × 512 ≈ 1.3 million. Recurrent: n·d² = 50 × 262,144 ≈ 13.1 million. Self-attention is about 10 times cheaper (illustrative arithmetic; big-O ignores constants). This matches the paper's point that it wins when n < d.

Open question. One alternative visible in Table 3 (B): smaller d_k also cuts parameters (65M to 58M or 60M), so lost capacity could explain the drop. A test: shrink d_k but add the parameters back elsewhere, then compare.
No. The paper only shows learned and sinusoidal encodings score about the same on the dev set (Table 3 E). A fair test would train on short sentences and evaluate on longer ones with both encodings.

Very long sequences, where n exceeds d (the paper mentions images, audio, and video as future targets). Proposed fix: restricted self-attention over a neighbourhood of size r, cost O(r·n·d), but maximum path length rises to O(n/r).

claim_notes.note: 'First' is the authors' own claim, qualified with 'to the best of our knowledge' (Sec. 2, p. 2).
Test set is newstest2014. Compare 28.4 against the ConvS2S Ensemble row (26.36) in Table 2.
Table 2 and the abstract say 41.8; Sec. 6.1 text says 41.0. Check both on pp. 1 and 8. The big EN-FR model used dropout 0.1, not the 0.3 listed for 'big' in Table 3.
FLOPs are the authors' estimate: training time × GPUs × assumed TFLOPS per GPU (footnote 5, p. 8), not a measurement.
These are asymptotic bounds. Table 1 does not give wall-clock times.
Only holds when n < d. For long sequences the n² term dominates; see the restricted self-attention row in Table 1.
The paper says 'we suspect'. No experiment isolates the scaling factor.
Dev set (newstest2013), no checkpoint averaging, single runs. Differences of a few tenths of BLEU may be noise; the paper reports no variance.
Parameters also change in these rows (58M, 60M vs 65M), which is another possible cause.
The extrapolation benefit is a stated hope; no experiment in the paper tests longer sequences.
Read rows (C) and (D) of Table 3. Bigger models also have more parameters and compute, so 'bigger is better' is not a controlled comparison.
Table 4 lists Luong et al. (multi-task, 93.0) and Dyer et al. (generative, 93.3) above 92.7. The text's 'all except RNNG' claim does not match the multi-task row.
